data.title: What Employers Are Actually Buying
data.excerpt: I spent the last two to three months looking for work, and partway through I started measuring what employers actually ask for in AI agent roles. The search totals lied. The job descriptions told a calmer, more useful story.

children.text: TLDR: I spent two to three months looking for work, and instead of trusting the noise on social media I read 128 real job descriptions for AI agent roles, in full, twice over. Employers are not hiring for a specific framework. They are hiring for agent building experience, and they say so plainly, usually with a list like “LangChain, LangGraph, LlamaIndex, or similar.” What they ask for around the framework matters more: evals, observability, security, and Python. The full report, with the tables and the method, is here:
What employers are actually buying
Why I ran this at all

I started looking for work in the middle of August, and like a lot of people I watched the agent framework conversation online and tried to work out which names were worth learning. The conversation is loud. One framework is declared dead on a Tuesday and essential by Friday, and the loudest signals, posts and likes and stars, turned out to be the least connected to hiring.

So I did the boring thing. I counted job postings on LinkedIn and a few other boards, and then, because the counts bothered me, I started reading the actual descriptions. That second step changed the conclusions, which is most of what this post is about. The search took a while, 137 applications over about two months, and it ended well. I start at BetterHelp in November. Partway through, the research stopped being a map of where to apply and became a list of what to get better at, and I think that second use is the more durable one.
The totals lied

The first pass was simple counting, and it produced confident numbers that did not survive contact with the postings themselves. LinkedIn caps the counts it displays, so four different frameworks can all show the same ceiling number, which makes any ranking between them an artifact of the display rather than a measurement. Reposts do the rest of the damage. The same role appears under a dozen locations, and recruiters copy each other, so one opening can look like twenty.

Keyword matching is worse. Searching for MCP surfaced maintenance and technician jobs. Searching for the full phrase “Model Context Protocol” surfaced model risk and model validation roles, which are about financial models and have nothing to do with agents. None of this is a conspiracy. It is just what keyword search over job boards produces, and it means the totals are, at best, weather. Directional, maybe. Not evidence.

NOTE: If you take one thing from this section, take this. A search result count is a count of pages that contain a string. It is not a count of jobs, and it is definitely not a count of what an employer is willing to pay for.
What I did instead

I read descriptions. The first validated pass covered 20 postings in full. The second, on October 28, covered 128 unique US postings from the previous 30 days, 91 from LinkedIn and 37 from company job boards, deduped by employer, title, and near identical text. For each one I recorded whether a framework was required, preferred, one of several alternatives, or simply mentioned, and I kept the excerpts that justified the call.

Two method choices mattered. First, the second pass searched by role, things like “agentic AI engineer,” rather than by framework keyword, which avoided most of the false positives. Second, the source mix moved the numbers. Company boards at AI first companies rarely name a framework at all. Only 3 of the 37 board postings asked for one, not counting MCP, while big companies and consultancies on LinkedIn list frameworks as a matter of habit. Any sample that leans on one source will inherit that source’s habits, and mine is no exception.
What employers are actually buying

The finding that held across both samples is simple. Employers do not require a framework. Of the 128 postings, exactly one named a single framework without listing alternatives, and even it mentioned others elsewhere in the text. Everything else reads as a bundle, a set of acceptable examples standing in for a skill the employer actually wants, which is building agents that survive production.

Within that, a leading group is real. LangGraph appeared in 44 of the 128 postings as required or preferred, LangChain in 40, and MCP in 36. CrewAI followed at 18, with LlamaIndex and AutoGen at 16 each, Semantic Kernel at 14, and Google ADK newly visible at 8. LangGraph edging LangChain surprised me a little, and LlamaIndex sitting lower than the first small sample suggested is a reminder of how much a sample of 20 can mislead. The honest summary is that the top three lead as a group, that most postings name several of them, and that treating the counts as separate piles of opportunity would double count the same jobs.

MCP deserves a word of its own, because it is not a framework. It is a protocol, and it shows up differently, usually as a concrete task: build MCP servers, maintain MCP servers, expose tools over MCP. It appeared at enterprises and at AI native companies alike, which almost nothing else did. If there is a single concrete skill in this data, that is the one.
What shows up besides a framework

This is the part I keep coming back to, because it is where the leverage is. Among the postings that named a framework, evals and observability appeared in 87 percent, security and governance in 83 percent, and Python in 84 percent. The unglamorous work, measuring whether the agent did the right thing and controlling what it is allowed to do, is what employers describe when they describe the job.

The infrastructure numbers corrected an earlier claim of mine. In the first sample of 20, Terraform appeared in 29 percent of framework postings, and I repeated that figure. In the sample of 128 it is 7 percent. Docker is 43 percent, FastAPI 24 percent, and Kubernetes 31 percent. Terraform still matters to me, but as platform depth, the thing that makes the rest deployable and repeatable, not as a headline hiring signal. Small samples produce big percentages, and I would rather correct that here than let it stand.

One more correction, in the other direction. n8n appears in zero of the 128 postings, down from 3 in the first sample, and that is not a decline. The second pass searched engineering roles. n8n lives in operations and automation roles, which this sample did not cover. Absence in a sample is only ever absence in that sample.
Where my own stack fits

I come from PHP and Laravel, with AWS and platform work, so I read this data with skin in the game. PHP appeared once in 128 postings, inside a list of languages. Whatever I hoped about a “Laravel plus AI” niche, the postings do not support it, and I would rather know that than pitch it.

What does hold up is a shape I already believed in. Laravel is a fine product layer. It is good at the application, the users, the billing, the boring and essential parts. The agents can live behind it in Python, and MCP is a clean boundary between the two, because the protocol does not care what language is on either side. That reading survived the data. The niche framing did not.
What this turned into

I took the BetterHelp role before the second sample ran, so this research is no longer a job hunt map for me. It reads better as a skills roadmap, and that is how I am using it now. Build MCP servers, because that is the most concrete ask in the data. Get serious about evals and guardrails in Python, because nearly every posting assumes them. Stay fluent in LangGraph and LangChain without marrying either, because employers treat them as interchangeable and I should too. Keep going with Kubernetes and Terraform, as platform depth rather than as a headline.

If you are earlier in the search than I am now, the practical version is shorter. Read twenty real descriptions for the roles you want before you learn anything new. The descriptions will tell you what is actually being bought, and it is rarely the thing the timeline is arguing about that week.

faq.question: What do employers hiring for AI agent roles actually ask for?
faq.answer: In a sample of 128 real job descriptions read in full, no framework was required on its own. Only 1 of 128 postings named a single framework without listing alternatives. Employers ask for agent building experience, usually naming a bundle like LangChain, LangGraph, LlamaIndex, or similar.

faq.question: Which agent framework appears most often in job postings?
faq.answer: LangGraph appeared in 44 of 128 postings as required or preferred, just ahead of LangChain at 40 and MCP at 36. The three lead as a group, and most postings that name one name several, so the counts overlap and should not be added together.

faq.question: What skills show up alongside frameworks in agent job postings?
faq.answer: Evals and observability appeared in 87 percent of the postings that named a framework, security and governance in 83 percent, and Python in 84 percent. Docker appeared in 43 percent and Kubernetes in 31 percent, while Terraform was only 7 percent, much lower than an earlier, smaller sample suggested.

faq.question: Why not just count LinkedIn search results?
faq.answer: The totals are not a measurement. LinkedIn caps its displayed counts, the same posting is reposted across locations and recruiters, and keyword matching pulls in unrelated jobs. MCP, for example, also matched maintenance technician roles. Reading the descriptions themselves is slower and far more honest.

faq.question: Does PHP or Laravel show up in AI agent job postings?
faq.answer: Almost never. PHP appeared once in 128 postings, inside a list of languages. My own read is that Laravel still works well as the product layer, with Python agents behind an MCP boundary, but the hiring market is not asking for it by name.

data.title: The Deliverable Isn't the App Anymore
data.excerpt: The app is only one piece of what a client needs now. The rest is the package around it: the repo as context hub, a shared room with an agent in it, evals from the start, CI/CD measured against the DORA metrics, and feature flags - and why a solo builder can offer the whole thing.
data.tag_order: ai, agents, automation, evals, cicd, dora, feature-flags

children.text: TLDR
TLDR:

Coding is cheap now. What a client actually needs - and what you can actually sell - is the app plus the operating environment around it: a shared room where they can talk to you and to the system, a repo that holds the code, the infrastructure, the decisions and the design guide, a safe way to query their own data, evals that are there from the start, a CI/CD pipeline you can measure against the DORA metrics, and feature flags so that deploying is not the same as releasing. You do not need to be a big agency to offer that. If you can build the app, you can build this package around it. Your job shifts from being the developer they send feature requests to, to being the architect of the patterns that let them explore and steer without breaking it.
The old handoff
For 25 years, the handoff looked pretty much the same.

I would build the thing. I would deploy the thing. I would write some documentation, or mean to write some documentation. Then I would hand over a URL and maybe a PDF, and the phone calls would start.
“How does the discount actually get calculated?” “Can we see everyone who signed up but never finished?” “Wait, why does it do that when…?”

Every one of those questions routed back through me. Not because the client could not think for themselves. Because the system was a black box to them. The answers lived in code they could not read, in infrastructure they could not see, and in decisions that were in my head, or in an email thread from three months ago.
And the documentation started going out of date the day I wrote it. The first change after handoff made part of it wrong, and nobody, including me, knew which part.
That model made sense when code was expensive. My value was that I could produce the code. A feature request would come in, and a feature would go out, and the time in between was mostly me typing.
Code is not expensive anymore. So if the code is not the scarce part, why are we still delivering like it is?
What I deliver now instead
Now the deliverable is a package, and the app is just one piece of it. Let me walk through the pieces, because each one looks small on its own and they only really make sense together.
1. The app, in a repo that holds everything

Not just the application code. The Terraform too, and the CI/CD, and a few folders I will come back to in a moment that matter more than they sound: a specs folder where the decisions live, and a design folder where the design guide lives.

One repo that describes the whole system. What it does, what it runs on, how it gets deployed, why it was built the way it was built, and what it is supposed to look like. If it is not in the repo, it did not happen. This is the context hub for this application.
2. A shared room

A Slack channel - it does not have to be Slack, any chat your client already lives in works - where the client, their team, and I are all in the same conversation. No ticket portal nobody checks. No separate email thread per person, where half the context is always in the thread you were not on.
This is where the work happens now. Questions, ideas, a “hey, I noticed this” on a Tuesday. All of it in one place, with the context building up as you go.
3. The AI, tagged into that room, connected to the repo

This is the piece that has been building across the last few posts, the ambient Slack agent and giving AI its own desk and computer. Claude is in that shared room, and it is connected to the GitHub repo holding the code and the Terraform and those folders I mentioned.
So it does not guess how the system works. It reads how the system works.

And each application basically gets a full agent with a desktop of its own, in the sense I talked about in the agents posts. A Linux machine, with Chrome, a shell, and files it can work with. So when a question in the room turns into real work - go look at this data, go run this process, go check what the system actually did - the agent is not limited to answering from the repo. It has a place to do the work, in the same way a person on the team would sit down at their computer and do it. The room is where you talk to it. The desktop is where it works.
The client can ask, in plain language:
“How do we handle it when a payment fails?” “Walk me through what happens when someone signs up.” “What would break if we changed this field?”
And the answer comes from the source itself. Not from a wiki I wrote six months ago. Not from my memory on a Tuesday afternoon.
4. A safe way to query their own data

Through MCP - the standard way you plug an AI into other tools and data sources - the client can connect to their own data, read-only and scoped to what they are allowed to see, and ask questions of it in that same room.

That used to be a feature request, and then a report build, and then a ticket, and then a wait. Now a lot of it is just a question. That is a bigger change than it sounds, especially for a small client who was never going to get a data team.
5. The guardrails

Evals, testing, CI/CD, and the security boundaries. Technically, what this is about is what runs, automatically, every time something changes or is proposed: the application tests, the eval cases for the AI parts, the checks in the pipeline before a deploy is allowed to happen, and the limits on what the AI and the data connections can reach - read-only here, nothing there, no secrets anywhere near it. It matters more in this setup than in a normal handoff because of the shape of the work itself. The client is going to be asking the system questions and proposing changes through it on a regular basis, not just at release time, so the checking cannot be a manual step that depends on me remembering to do it. It has to be in the pipeline, running the same way every time, whether I am at my desk or not. I will go through the pieces of it in the sections below.
The repo is more than code: specs and design
I want to pull on those two folders for a minute, because they are easy to skip, and skipping them is how this whole thing quietly falls apart.
A specs folder, for decisions.

Every system has decisions baked into it that are not visible in the code. Why does the refund work this way and not that way. Why did we choose this provider. What is the business rule when these two things conflict. In the old model, those decisions lived in meeting notes, in email, and mostly in my head, and they left when I left.
Now they go in a
specs/
folder in the repo, in plain language, versioned with everything else. When a decision changes, the spec changes, in a pull request, where you can see what the old thinking was and what replaced it.
This matters for the AI too, not just for the humans. When the client asks “why does it work this way,” the code can only tell them
how
it works. The spec is where the
why
is. Without it, the AI in the room can describe the machinery and still miss the point of the machinery, which is the part the client actually cares about.
A design folder, for the design guide.
Same idea, on the visual side. Colors, type, spacing, the components we use and how we use them, example screens. That goes in a
design/
folder in the repo, as a guide the AI can read, instead of living in a Figma file only one person can open, or worse, in nothing at all.

So when a new feature gets built, by me or with the AI helping, it does not come back looking like it belongs to a different product. It follows the guide, because the guide is right there in the same place as everything else. And when the client asks why something looks the way it does, or wants to change a pattern everywhere at once, there is one place to change it.

Neither folder is a big lift. A spec can start as a few paragraphs in plain English. A design guide can start as a page. What matters is that they exist, in the repo, from early on, instead of being reconstructed later from memory. Because reconstructed from memory is exactly the old model again.
Documentation that does not go out of date

Traditional documentation is a copy of the truth. Copies drift. The code changes, the copy does not, and pretty soon the copy is out of date and still being quoted back to you as if it were current, which is worse than no documentation at all.
When the AI answers from the repo - the actual code, the actual Terraform, the actual specs, the actual tests - there is no copy. The answer is put together from the source, at the moment you ask.

Change the code, or change a spec, and the next answer reflects the change. There is nothing separate to remember to update. And the notes that do need writing, the why behind a decision, the constraints, what good looks like, those now live with the code, versioned with the code, instead of on a wiki page nobody has opened since 2023.
Evals, from the start

This is the section I most want to get right, because I think evals are usually talked about as something you add later, once the system is built, if you have time. In this package they are there from the start, and there is a reason for that.

These systems are non-deterministic. I wrote a whole piece on this in the agents post: run an agent twenty times and it might not go the same way every time. Ask an AI the same question about a system next month, after the model has changed, or the prompt has changed, or the context has grown, and you may get a different answer. So how do you trust it?
You use evaluations. And you cannot bolt that on at the end, because by then you have no baseline. You have a feeling that it works, and a feeling is what you had on day one too.

So from the start, before the client is relying on any of this, we write down what has to stay true. Not in abstract terms. In their terms. The real questions they ask. The real searches they expect to work. The cases where the wrong answer would actually hurt.

“A new signup with a duplicate email should never create two accounts.” “Asking how refunds work should always mention the 14 day window.” “This search, with this spelling, should find this customer.”

That set is small at first. Five cases is fine. But it exists, and it runs, and it gives you a read on two things at once: whether the system is still doing what it is supposed to do, and what that is costing, so you can find the cheapest model and setup that still passes.
Then comes the part that makes it more than a test suite. It becomes a feedback cycle.

It goes like this. The client asks something in the room. The answer comes back, and it is close, but not quite how they actually do it. Maybe it missed a step in their process, maybe it described the rule the way the code does it and not the way the business thinks about it. In the old model, that correction evaporated. Someone would say “oh, actually…” in a call, and the system would go on being wrong in the same quiet way.

Here, the correction does two jobs. It updates the context - a spec gets clarified, a note gets added - and it becomes a new eval case. That exact question, with that exact expectation, now runs every time something changes. The system does not just get fixed once. It stays fixed, and you can prove it stays fixed, because the case is sitting in CI watching for it.
And that cycle is also where the prompts get written, which is the other half of this.

There is a drafting area for prompts: the shared room, plus a place in the repo where prompt drafts live, in plain language, where the client and I can work on them together. This matters more than most builders expect. The prompt is not a technical artifact. It is where the client’s real knowledge goes - how they talk to their customers, what the AI should always check, what it should never offer, when it should stop and hand the question to a human. The client is the expert on most of that, not me. If the prompt lives buried in code that only I can touch, that expertise never really gets in.

So we draft in the open. We try a version against the eval set. We look at where it did well and where it missed, and we adjust the wording, and we run it again. The iteration is visible to the client, and it is in their language, so they can steer it the way they would steer a new employee’s handbook, because that is closer to what it is.

NOTE: I do not like putting the live prompt in code, because I want to be able to update a prompt without a deploy. Keep the prompt somewhere you can edit it. The drafting area is where new versions are worked on and tested. A draft only becomes the live prompt once it passes the evals.

Do you see the loop now? Real use creates corrections. Corrections become evals and better drafts. Better drafts pass the gate and go live. And the next round of real use starts from a better place than the last one. That is how a system like this gets better over time instead of slowly drifting, which is what happened to every hand-off-and-walk-away system I ever built.
CI/CD, and what DORA taught us about doing this well
If evals are the gate for the AI parts, CI/CD is the gate for everything, and it belongs in the deliverable, not behind the scenes where the client never sees it.
I have been writing about building your own stack, and this is where that work pays off for a client. The pipeline I use is GitHub Actions, and for a typical system it looks like this:

content.code:
pull request
    |
    v
tests run (against a real Postgres and Redis, not mocks of them)
    |
    v
formatting / lint checks
    |
    v
evals run, for the AI parts of the system
    |
    v
the production Docker image is built - the exact image that will ship
    |
    v
push to main, and only if all of the above passed
    |
    v
deploy: migrations, health checks, switch traffic to the new release
    |
    v
the previous release stays right there, ready to switch back to

children.text: A few things in there are doing more work than they look like. GitHub connects to the cloud account using OIDC, so there is no long-lived access key sitting in a settings page waiting to leak. The image that gets deployed is the image that got tested, not a rebuild that is probably the same. Migrations run as part of the release, and health checks decide whether the new release actually gets traffic.

Now, why do I care about the shape of this pipeline, beyond “it is tidy”? Because there is research on what separates teams that ship software well from teams that struggle with it, and it is not opinion. It is DORA - dora.dev - the group that has been measuring this for years, and that work became the book
Accelerate
. Elite teams, as they call them, are not the ones with the most process. They are the ones that do well on four measures:
Deployment frequency.
How often you put code into production. Elite teams deploy on demand, many times a day if they want to. Struggling teams deploy monthly and hold their breath when they do.
Lead time for changes.

How long it takes for a commit to get to production. Elite is under a day, and it used to be measured in hours. Struggling is weeks of a change waiting in queues and approvals that are not actually checking anything.
Change failure rate.
What share of your deployments cause a problem in production that needs a fix or a rollback. Lower is better, and elite teams keep this small, largely because their changes are small.
Time to restore service.
When something does go wrong, how long until it is working again. Elite is under an hour.

That last one is the one I want you to notice, because it answers the question every client is really asking, which is not “will it ever break.” Of course it might. Sure, a bug might go to prod. Testing and evals and a good pipeline make that less likely, and make the changes smaller when it happens, but no honest setup promises it can never happen, and you should be suspicious of anyone who does.

The real confidence is this: if a bug does get to production, you find out in moments, from health checks and from a client who is in the room with the system all day, and you fix it in moments. The previous release is still there, so switching back is a switch, not a rescue operation. Or you fix forward, through the same pipeline, and because the pipeline is automated and the lead time is short, “fix forward” means minutes, not a weekend.

That is why small, frequent changes beat big, rare ones, and it is why the DORA numbers matter even for a team of one. A solo builder with a real pipeline, real tests, and an eval set can operate at the elite end of those four measures. A bigger team deploying by hand once a month cannot, no matter how many people they have. The measures do not care about your headcount. They care about your pipeline and your habits.

And this is what lets me let a client steer. A change they propose goes in as a pull request, the tests and evals run, a human reviews it, and it deploys the same way everything else deploys. If it turns out to be wrong in production, we are not in trouble, we are in a routine. We switch back, we look at what happened, and very often that failure becomes - you guessed it - a new test, and a new eval case, so that particular thing cannot quietly happen again.
Feature flags: deploying is not the same as releasing
One more piece that sits right next to CI/CD, and it is a simple one, but it changes how safe a release feels.

A feature flag is a switch around a piece of new code. The code can be merged and deployed to production with the switch off, which means it is sitting there, in the real system, and nobody using the system can see it or is affected by it. Deploying and releasing become two different decisions, with time in between them if you want it.

You do not need a special platform for this. Whatever framework you are building in will have an option for it: Laravel has Pennant, Rails has Flipper, and most other stacks have a library that does the same job, and there are services that will run the switches for you if you would rather have a dashboard. For most systems I build, the library in the framework is enough to start.

The way it gets used in this package looks like this. A new feature goes through the normal path: pull request, tests and evals, deploy, with the flag off. Then we turn the flag on for just us - my account, the client’s team, a QA account - and use it in the real production system, not a staging copy of it. The automated checks can run against the flagged path too, so production itself gets tested, with real data and real infrastructure, while the public is still on the old path.
If that looks right, we turn it on for a small segment: one client site, or a small percentage of users, and we watch it there. Then, when it has earned it, we turn it on for everyone.

And if it has not earned it - if something is wrong, or the client tries it and says this is not what we meant - turning it off is flipping the switch back. No redeploy, no rollback of the release, no scramble. The code stays deployed and dormant, we fix what needs fixing, and we try again. That is time to restore measured in seconds, and it is one more reason the DORA conversation and this model belong together.

For the client, this is often the piece that makes the whole thing feel safe enough to actually use. A feature they proposed can be in their hands, in their real system, for them to test and react to, before any of their customers ever see it. Their feedback at that stage is the best kind, because it is based on the real thing, and it feeds straight back into the cycle I described in the evals section.

One bit of discipline to go with it: flags are temporary. Once a feature is fully released and settled, take the flag and the old path out, and note it in the specs. A system that collects old switches and dead paths gets confusing for everyone, including the AI answering questions about it, and confusing is exactly what this whole package is trying to avoid.
The risks
I do not want to sell this as magic, because it is not, and the risks are real. I would rather name them in front of the client. That tends to build more trust than pretending they do not exist.
Data access has to be scoped and read-only by default.

Connecting an AI to a client’s database through MCP is powerful, and powerful cuts both ways. Read-only. Least-privilege. Only the tables and views they need. Writes are a separate, deliberate decision, if ever.
Secrets and Terraform state never go in what the AI can read.
Not in the repo, not in the room, not in a prompt. The AI needs the code, the specs, and the shape of the infrastructure. It never needs the keys to it.
The shared room is a no-sensitive-data room, by rule.

Chat platforms are US-hosted third parties. So we set the rule on day one: no passwords, no dumps of personal data, no sensitive records in chat. The room is for talking about the system. The system itself holds the sensitive stuff, behind its own permissions.
Client changes only land as pull requests through the gate.
I covered this above, but it belongs on the risks list too, because every incident version of this story starts with someone skipping that step, just this once.
If you cannot do those things, do not offer this yet. If you can - and they are mostly discipline, not new technology - you are most of the way there.
What this does to the business model
Project fees fit the old model: build it, hand it over, wave goodbye, wait for the next project.

This package does not fit that, because this package wants a relationship. The feedback cycle I described does not run itself. Someone has to tend the evals, keep the specs current, look at the pipeline when it complains, and be in the room when a question turns into a decision.

The clients I work with were already asking for this, I think. I just did not have a name for it. They do not really want a vendor they file tickets with. They want a steward, someone who set the system up right in the first place and is still paying attention to it. That is a retainer, a smaller ongoing relationship instead of a big build and a disappearance. The system keeps getting better at the things they care about, because their corrections keep feeding back into it, and I get predictable work on systems I know deeply, instead of starting from zero every quarter.
A starter version, if you want to try this
You do not have to build all of it at once. The smallest version I would call real looks like this:
One repo: the app code and the Terraform, a
specs/
folder you start on day one even if it is only a page, and a
design/
folder with whatever design guide you have, even if that starts as a page too

GitHub Actions from the first deploy, not added later: tests on every pull request, the production image built in CI, and a deploy you do not do by hand - plus the feature flag library from your framework, so new features can deploy switched off and be released to the client, then a small segment, then everyone
Five evals, written at the start, from the five questions your client will ask most - and a prompt drafting area, even if that is just a folder in the repo and the shared room
One shared chat room with your client, with the AI tagged in and connected to that repo, read-only
One read-only, scoped MCP connection, to the piece of data the client asks about constantly
The four rules, written down and put in the room on day one: scoped data, no secrets in reach, no sensitive data in chat, changes only as pull requests
That is a full-stack offer. Not a demo version of one. You can grow every piece of it from there, and it will grow, because the feedback cycle starts turning as soon as a real client starts using it.
The takeaway
I used to think my deliverable was the app.

It is not, and it has not been for a while. I just could not deliver the rest of it without a team and a budget nobody had. Now I can: one builder, good patterns, a real pipeline, and a client who can ask their own system how it works, and why it works that way, and get an answer that comes from the system itself.

The deliverable is not the app anymore. It is the confidence to use it, to change it, and to keep asking it questions, knowing there is a gate in front of production and a way back if something slips through.

If you build for clients, I would start with one small system and try the package on it. Get the repo in shape, get the pipeline running, write the first five evals before you think you need them. You will learn more from one real client using it than from planning a bigger version of it.
Questions, ask below. Topics you want covered, ask below. Thank you.

faq.question: Isn't this just handing the client a chatbot?
faq.answer: No. A chatbot bolted onto an app answers from whatever you fed it, and it drifts out of date as the app changes. This is the AI connected to the repo that is the system: the code, the Terraform, the specs and design guide, and the tests, plus a scoped, read-only way to query real data, all inside the room where the work already happens. The grounding is the difference.

faq.question: Why do evals need to be there from the start, instead of added later?
faq.answer: Because without them you have no baseline. These systems are non-deterministic, and models, prompts and context all change over time, so a month from now you will have no way to tell whether an answer got better or worse except by feel. Evals written at the start give you something to run every change against. They also capture client corrections as permanent cases, so a fix stays fixed.

faq.question: What is the prompt drafting area, in practice?
faq.answer: A shared place - the client room, plus prompt drafts kept in the repo in plain language - where you and the client work on what the AI is told: how it should answer, what it should check, what it should never do, and when it should hand off to a human. Drafts are tested against the eval set before they become the live prompt, and the live prompt is kept somewhere you can edit without a deploy.

faq.question: What are the DORA metrics, and why are they in a piece about working solo?
faq.answer: They are the four measures from dora.dev research on software delivery: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and time to restore service. They are in here because they are mostly about pipeline and habits, not team size. A solo builder with GitHub Actions, small changes, and automated deploys and rollbacks can sit at the elite end of all four.

faq.question: So can a bug still get to production?
faq.answer: Yes, and any setup that promises otherwise is not being straight with you. Testing, evals, and small changes make it less likely and less serious. What the pipeline really buys you is recovery: health checks surface it quickly, the previous release is still available to switch back to, and a fix can go through the same automated path in minutes. Time to restore is a design choice, not luck.

faq.question: What are feature flags doing in this package?
faq.answer: They separate deploying from releasing. New code goes to production with the flag off, so nobody is affected. Then it is switched on for the builder and the client team first, so it can be tested manually and automatically in the real system, then for a small segment of users, and only then for everyone. If something is wrong, turning the flag off restores the old behavior in seconds, without a redeploy. Most frameworks have a flag library - Laravel has Pennant, Rails has Flipper - so it does not need a separate platform to start.

faq.question: What goes in the specs folder, and what goes in the design folder?
faq.answer: The specs folder holds the decisions, in plain language: the business rules, why a provider or an approach was chosen, what should happen when rules conflict. The design folder holds the design guide: colors, type, spacing, components and how they are used, and example screens. Both live in the repo, versioned, so the humans and the AI are working from the same source.

faq.question: Can the client break production with this?
faq.answer: Not if the gate is built right. Clients explore and propose. Changes land only as pull requests, through tests and evals, with a human review, and they deploy through the same pipeline as everything else. And if a change does cause a problem, the previous release is there to switch back to.

faq.question: What data can the AI actually see?
faq.answer: Only what you scope it to. Read-only data access through MCP, least-privilege, and never secrets or Terraform state. Deciding those boundaries is a core part of the builder's job in this model.

faq.question: I'm a solo developer. Can I really offer all of this?
faq.answer: I think so, and that is kind of the point of the piece. The code is the cheap part now. With solid starter patterns for auth, infrastructure, GitHub Actions, and hosting, one builder can deliver the app plus the environment around it. What you are selling is the patterns, the guardrails, and the stewardship, not a headcount.

faq.question: What replaces project fees in this model?
faq.answer: For most clients, a retainer: ongoing responsibility for the pipeline, the evals, the specs, and being in the room, instead of a one-off build and a handoff. It is the relationship a lot of clients were already asking for, just named and structured.

data.title: Giving AI Its Own Desk and Computer
data.excerpt: Giving AI its own workspace makes browser-heavy tasks easier to hand off. From recovering $1,600 in solar payments to turning a research workflow into an API, here is where agents in a box are useful.

children.text: TLDR
TLDR:

Give AI its own desk and computer, then give it a specific job. These environments make it easier to hand off browser work, run recurring tasks, and let other applications request that work through an API. I see them as an addition to the AI tools we already use.

Think of it as giving AI its own desk and computer, as if it were a coworker. It has a browser, files, and software to get work done. Then imagine telling it, “By the way, you can also have multiple agents working under you that you can manage.”

That is the idea behind what I’m calling “AI agents in a box.” The desk is an analogy, and the exact setup varies, but the important part is that the AI has a workspace where it can keep doing the work you give it.
Grok Bot
describes teams of agents working on a shared cloud computer, while
Muse
has its own dedicated computer in the cloud.
Grokked Bot
is my open-source project for running this kind of setup under our own control, with each bot in its own container. Coordinating those bots as a team is still on its roadmap.
You may hear people call these systems a “harness.” That just means the software around the AI model: the interface, tools, and environment that let it get work done.
There are two areas where this interests me: personal use and business use.
What made it click for me
For me, it was the browser interaction.
Claude Desktop failed numerous times trying to get things done in the browser.
Astra
crushed some of those same tasks, but sometimes it was in my way because I was using the computer too. On mobile, the experience was hit or miss.
To be fair, it is already amazing that these tools can do this work. But giving the AI its own computer removed another hurdle. It could work in its browser while I continued working in mine.

I see these systems as an addition to the AI tools we already use. Some tasks involve a lot of clicking through websites, gathering information, downloading files, and moving between systems. Having somewhere to send that work is useful.
And once the process works, you can go further. You can schedule it or give another application a way to request it.
Personal use: recovering $1,600 in solar payments
Our house came with solar panels. We had not been receiving money owed to us for SRECs, or solar renewable energy certificates, and I was not familiar with how any of this worked.

There was a website and a series of support emails explaining the process, but it was not clear. Responses were also slow. By the time an answer arrived a week later, it was hard to pick up the thread and remember what we were waiting for.
That is the kind of detail work that takes energy. You have to go back through the emails, revisit the website, and figure out the next step every time.
I put an agent on it.

It went through the emails, navigated the website, reviewed our contracts to verify the process, and handled the forms and email conversation. That included asking the right questions and answering the questions support sent back.
I let it do the work. The solar setup came with the house, and figuring all of this out myself was exactly the task I needed help with.
Within a week, we had a $1,600 refund.

Now it is set up to monitor the dates when we expect reimbursement and check our bank transactions through Plaid to see whether the payment arrived. Yes, I am comfortable giving it that access. If the payment does not arrive in time, it emails support.
It also checks our electrical bill to make sure we are receiving the monthly credits from the electric company.

What this means is that I have help following through on something I would otherwise have to keep remembering to check. There are emails, contracts, a website, payments, and bills involved. Giving the agent a place to work across those things made a real difference for me.
Help with the detail work
Another example is some college work I’m doing to get a degree.

The agent helps me go through the class website, gather assignments, and organize what is due when. It helps identify comments and conversations I need to reply to and review my work against the class expectations.
That makes it easier to fit school around a full-time job and still have time for other things.

I have also used this approach to combine information from an event website with travel plans. The information was tedious to gather and organize, but having it brought together made the scheduling much easier.
These are ordinary tasks. They are also tasks that can sit there because I do not want to spend my available energy sorting through all the details.
Business use: making an API with an agent behind it
A clear business example involved someone downloading FEC donation data for research.

Their routine was to go to a site, apply filters, work through the pages of results, download the file, and put it into our system. They knew how to do it, but they still had to repeat those steps each time they needed the data.
Once they showed the agent the process, it could do that work for them.
Then they took it a step further and enabled a webhook, giving our main application an endpoint where it could send requests to the agent.
What started as a task someone performed in a browser became something our application could ask to have done.
Basically, they made an API with an agent behind it.

This is interesting to me as a builder. A staff member understands a process because they already do it as part of their job. They can show the agent that process, get it working, and then we can connect it to other tools.
The request might come from our application, from Slack, or from a schedule.
“Every Monday, download the data files from this site and upload them to our S3 bucket.”
That is a concrete job someone can hand off. For operations teams and businesses with repetitive browser work, those jobs add up.
Each employee can have a group of agents
This is what I mean when I say each staff person could have an army of agents.
One agent gathers research data. Another checks for missing payments. Another prepares a recurring report. Another handles requests from an internal application.
Each has a specific job and the context needed to do it.
The employee does not need to invent an entirely new way of working. They can start with a process they already understand and spend time helping the agent do it reliably.
Once that works, the process can become available to the rest of the business through a schedule or an integration.
The computer can also be a development environment
Giving the agent its own machine has another advantage.

In our case, it was running Linux, so the user could ask it to set up the software we use. From there, they could prompt it to build new features, QA the changes, and ship them through our existing process.
They did not have to first turn their own PC or Mac into a development environment.
That removes a hurdle for someone who understands the business and knows what they want the software to do, but does not want to spend their time setting up development tools.
The same idea applies to other software. If I want help processing a file or editing a video, the agent has an environment where it can install and run the necessary tools.
Yes, my Mac can do those things too. But now I have somewhere to send the task without first arranging everything on the computer I’m using.
Where the agent runs
Running locally meant we did not have another cloud environment to host and secure. We still had to decide what the agent could access, but the machine was under our control.
If you use a laptop that you close or take with you, a hosted environment has an advantage. The agent can keep working while your laptop is offline. That is part of the appeal of Grok Bot and Muse.

Grokked Bot also gives us the option to host the environment ourselves, including on a cloud machine. Its Tailscale integration gives us a way to reach its webhooks from other devices on our private network.

For this article, I’m assuming you are already comfortable using hosted AI models. Running the agent’s computer locally and running the model locally are separate decisions. A local computer can still send information to the model provider you choose.
From a business standpoint, I see the agent’s permissions as closely tied to the employee’s permissions. Giving someone an agent should not automatically expand what they are allowed to access or do.
Why model choice matters
OpenRouter is another reason Grokked Bot interests me.

In my opinion, basing all your AI solutions around one vendor right now is risky. Models have limitations, some are expensive, and services go down. New models come out that you want to try. Older models get deprecated when you would have been happy to keep using them.
As a business, I want room to make those decisions as things change.
OpenRouter
provides access to models from different providers through a common API. That gives us a way to change model choices without building a separate integration for each provider.
I also want to choose the model based on the work. If each employee has several agents, there is no reason to assume every agent needs the same model at the same cost.
Those costs matter as more people start using these systems for recurring work.

Then there are evaluations, or evals: checking how well the AI is doing the job. I consider those a key part of building with AI. When another model is helping judge the results, I want the option to use one from a different model family. I do not want all our judging tied to the same family of models doing the work.

Model choice does not eliminate outages or keep a deprecated model available forever. Changing a model still means checking that it performs the task well. But I want that flexibility built into the system.
Start with a task you already have
If you want a place to start, try giving Muse a job-search task across Indeed and other well-known job portals it can access.

Tell it what kind of work you are looking for, your experience, and the constraints that matter to you, such as location, salary, or remote work. Ask it to gather relevant openings and explain why each one might fit.
That gives you a concrete way to explore the idea. There are websites to visit, details to gather, and information to compare.
For me, these setups are making it easier to get started. Knowing what is possible is becoming the new challenge.

Someone might recognize that an agent can download a file for them, but not yet realize that the same process can become something their application requests automatically. Or that the agent’s computer can also be a place to build and test a new feature.
Give it a desk, give it a specific job, and see how much of that work you can hand over.

faq.question: What is an AI agent in a box?
faq.answer: It is an AI agent with a working environment that includes a browser, files, and software. Depending on the product, it can also run scheduled tasks, receive requests from applications, and work alongside other agents.

faq.question: Does this replace ChatGPT or Claude Desktop?
faq.answer: I see these systems as an addition to the tools we already use. A separate workspace is useful when a task involves substantial browser work and you want to keep using your own computer.

faq.question: Can an application send work to an agent?
faq.answer: Yes. In the research workflow described here, a webhook lets the main application request data collection from an agent that performs the browser steps and brings the file into our system.

faq.question: Does running an agent locally mean the AI model runs locally?
faq.answer: No. The agent's computer and the model are separate choices. A local agent can still send information to a hosted model provider.

faq.question: Why does model choice matter for a business?
faq.answer: Different tasks have different cost and capability needs. Model choice also helps a business adapt when providers change their offerings and compare results using models from different families.

data.title: Why You Should Learn to Build Your Own Stack
data.excerpt: Managed services are great until the bill and the environments pile up. I'm starting a series on building your own stack — Terraform, Docker, CI, deploy — so you can stand up predictable, secure places to run the apps you're wiring together.
data.tag_order: devops, terraform, docker, laravel, aws, digitalocean, infrastructure-as-code, self-hosting

children.text: TLDR:

I’m starting a series on how to self-host your own stack. By “stack” I mean the combination of resources that host your application — linux box, database, queue, storage, DNS, maybe a load balancer later. Services like Railway and Supabase are amazing. They also add up money wise and more importanlty knowing how to connect your intranet into managed agents and other systems is key. By the end of this first lesson we’ll have one command that builds a classic stack you can deploy to: infrastructure as code, CI after tests, automatic deploy, zero downtime, no clickOps.
This is post one in a series: how to self-host your own stack.
Why learning to build your own stack matters
NOTE: if you get stuck just chat with the code base. Open up Claude or Codex or whatever and just ask your question

I use services like Railway and Supabase and I might use a queue system like Redis etc. Later on maybe a load balancer. Storage, authentication, websockets — a lot of that I get out of Supabase but running your own Supabase can be a lot.
These are amazing services. They can also add up. Supabase isn’t free after your first few stacks. And when building the company intranet with multiple environments it will add up.

So how do we use tools like Terraform (and later Kubernetes) to quickly stand up what I call different types of stacks — that combination of resources — with predictable pricing? And then how do we get our code there easily.

This matters even more as we try to integrate all these other systems together. For example Claude Managed Agents might need to access a file on your storage area, or a service. Containers are key too so you can keep them more up to date and scale. Even if you go back to Vercel + Supabase + GitHub Actions etc it is still great to know these things.
What I mean by stack (and what this series is not)
This isn’t going to be about Stripe integration and things like that. This is more for intranet applications that you’re building for internal business use.
When we deploy these stacks, we start simple.
The first one is a simple Terraform command that builds up our stack on AWS (later Azure and Google Cloud). What we end up with is a very predictable pricing stack.

You could go a couple of ways: dedicated databases, dedicated queue systems from the cloud. Or we can just use something like an EC2 — a Linux box basically. We’ll try a whole bunch of them. Every cloud provider. Later I will start to use Kubernetes to more easily manage the running services and scale as needed.
By the time we’re done with this first lesson, we’re going to have one command, and we’re going to build a system we can deploy to.
Classic path:
Infrastructure as code
CI — continuously pushing code and integrating it after tests into our trunk
Automatically deploy to that system
I will have trainings videos on all of this. First we build the stack. Then we enjoy deploying to the stack by pushing the code there.
We’ll have zero downtime during the deployments. Migrations with basically no touch. No need to click. No clickOps. All infrastructure as code.
Why Docker

We’re going to use Docker. It’s just amazing because we can run these locally, mess around locally, see our stuff working, and then deploy it. Even more importantly: we just won’t care as much when our Linux box is out of date. We can update it without worrying about breaking our application or the queue system or whatever.

This is going to be a stack based on Laravel to start, Postres as the database, Redis for queueing, and storage will be a “volume” we can backup and share as needed. Horizon so we can do queue jobs for us. GitHub actions will do all the Continuas Integration and Deployment, migrations will be in code.

Later on we’ll get into Kubernetes. Right now I’m just trying to keep it simple. I want to grow through this together — and I mean grow, because we’re going to be learning and changing and doing. AI ops is fun again, in my opinion.

Yes, you’ll need to know some basic Linux stuff. Don’t worry about it. You always have AI to help out. It can be wrong. It’s still amazing. You might get stuck on SSH. Ask AI. Or ask below - I’ll try to help you.
Where is the code
The code’s all on GitHub. When you pull it down you can run your Terraform in it to get going and set up the infrastructure requirements. Kind of like
npm init
— hey, give me what I need to run this.
We’ll focus first on an AWS system but again we will do Azure, GCP and maybe some others
Build it (the short version for this draft)
This repo will have the code.
https://github.com/alnutile/labs
you can:
Then follow the
labs/classic-stack/README.md
Read the script files to just see how things come together
This will get your docker running with the php and other elements needed for the initial web application.
Yes Laraval has Sail but I want to really show and see how this works so we can later move into Kubernetes etc. Keep in mind this is about hosting your own stack, any type.
The
labs/classic-stack/README.md
also notes
Local PostgreSQL/Redis use named volumes with no published database ports. The source and local reports are in
app/
; production reports use a separate persistent volume.
app/.env
is ignored. To change the local web port, set
APP_PORT
and
APP_URL
there.
down -v
deletes the local database and queue volumes.
This is pretty neat since docker can talk to other services running in it’s own internal network.
Building the Server
Ok now the README.md will cover this part and it starts off with:
PRICING:

The first version costs roughly $22 per month before taxes and optional backups when left running continuously in AWS us-west-2. That includes one small EC2 instance, a 30 GB encrypted gp3 disk, and one public IPv4 address. PostgreSQL, Redis, Horizon, Caddy, and Laravel all run as containers on that same machine, so they do not create separate service charges.

This is an estimate, not a fixed bill. Data transfer, snapshots, extra storage, CPU- credit usage, Cloudflare features, and domain registration can add to it. Stopping or destroying the instance reduces compute costs, but the disk, snapshots, and public IP may still incur charges depending on what remains.

$22 USD might seem high but what will happen shortly is we can run as many applications we want on this. Or use a smaller instance etc. This is a fixed cost that will not go up until the machine is maxed out which you will see can hold more than you think.

content.code:
export AWS_PROFILE=sundance        # replace with your profile
aws sts get-caller-identity
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/classic-stack-deploy -C classic-stack-deploy
cd terraform
cp terraform.tfvars.example terraform.tfvars

children.text: Since at this point we want to make sure we can get into the server after.
If you get stuck in a terminal sceen try pressing “q”
And when it asks for a passphrase just click “Return” since none is needed.
You will need your public ip try this:
Run curl -4
https://api.ipify.org

to find the public IPv4 address AWS will see. Add /32 because only that single address should be allowed to SSH into the server. Don’t use your local Wi-Fi address, and don’t open SSH to 0.0.0.0/0. If you’re using a VPN or your ISP changes your address, run the command again and update Terraform.
To get your SSH key into your clipboard do:
cat ~/.ssh/classic-stack-deploy.pub | pbcopy
Deploy from Github
Once the server is running, the deployment path becomes simple:

content.code:
pull request
    ↓
tests against PostgreSQL and Redis
    ↓
Docker image build
    ↓
push to main
    ↓
temporary SSH access for the GitHub runner
    ↓
upload the release to EC2
    ↓
run migrations and health checks
    ↓
switch the running application

children.text: The GitHub Actions workflow lives at the repository root in .github/workflows/classic- stack.yml.

Every pull request runs the application tests, Laravel Pint, a real Redis and Horizon queue check, and a production Docker image build. A push to main follows the same path. After the tests pass, the deployment job uploads the exact image that was tested.

The workflow uses GitHub’s OIDC connection to AWS, so there is no long-lived AWS access key stored in GitHub. AWS trusts only this repository’s production environment. During deployment, the workflow discovers the runner’s current public IP and temporarily adds that single /32 address to a dedicated SSH security group. The rule is removed when the job finishes.
The deployment connects using a dedicated deploy SSH key. It uploads an immutable release directory containing the Docker image and deployment files. On the server, the release script:
Starts PostgreSQL and Redis.
Runs Laravel migrations.
Starts the new application container.
Checks that the application can reach PostgreSQL and Redis.
Starts the new Horizon and scheduler processes.
Reloads Caddy with the new application upstream.
Drains and stops the previous application container.
NOTE: as you follow the
README
in the code base commands like STACK_HOST=$(terraform -chdir=terraform output -raw elastic_ip) is how you set a variable in the terminal. But if you change terminals that variable is gone.
The result is a controlled deployment without a planned web outage. The previous release remains available for rollback, and the current and previous symlinks show which releases are active.

This is near-zero-downtime deployment on one server. It is not high availability. A failed EC2 host, a full disk, an incompatible database migration, or a bad infrastructure change still affects the application. Database migrations must remain compatible with both the old and new application versions while traffic moves between them.
After the initial setup, deploying an update is simply:

content.code:
git add .
git commit -m "Update the application"
git push origin main

children.text: GitHub runs the tests first. Only a successful run is allowed to deploy.
CloudFlare
The hostname for this stack is
classic-stack.dailyai.studio
. Rather than clicking a DNS record into existence, Terraform manages the record alongside the AWS infrastructure.
The Cloudflare provider uses a narrowly scoped API token with Zone / DNS / Edit permission:

content.code:
printf 'Cloudflare token: '
read -rs CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN
echo

export TF_VAR_cloudflare_api_token="$CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN"

terraform -chdir=terraform plan -out classic-stack-with-dns.tfplan
terraform -chdir=terraform apply classic-stack-with-dns.tfplan

unset TF_VAR_cloudflare_api_token CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN

children.text: The Terraform resource is deliberately DNS-only while the server is coming online:

content.code:
resource "cloudflare_record" "classic_stack" {
count = local.cloudflare_enabled ? 1 : 0

zone_id = data.cloudflare_zone.classic_stack[0].id
name    = var.cloudflare_record_name
type    = "A"
value   = aws_eip.classic_stack.public_ip
ttl     = 1
proxied = var.cloudflare_record_proxied
}

children.text: DNS-only lets Caddy obtain the origin certificate directly. After HTTPS works, Cloudflare proxying can be enabled with cloudflare_record_proxied = true. When proxying, use Full (strict) SSL/TLS.

If the record already exists, import it into Terraform state before applying the plan. That turns the existing dashboard record into an infrastructure-as-code resource instead of creating a duplicate.
Make a User and Check it out
Registration is disabled in production, so create the first account over SSH:

content.code:
ssh -i ~/.ssh/classic-stack-deploy \
deploy@$(terraform -chdir=terraform output -raw elastic_ip)

children.text: Then run this on the server:

content.code:
export APP_ROOT=/home/deploy/apps/classic-stack
export RELEASE_ID=$(basename "$(readlink "$APP_ROOT/current")")


cd "$APP_ROOT/current"

docker compose \
--env-file "$APP_ROOT/shared/env/production.env" \
-p "release-$RELEASE_ID" \
-f deploy/compose.release.yaml \
exec --user www-data app \
php artisan stack:user you@example.com --name="Your Name"

children.text: Laravel will prompt for a password without echoing it. Add that same email to HORIZON_ALLOWED_EMAILS if the user should access /horizon.
Whats Next
Now lets make this computer really pay for itself. In the next post will will host 10 applications and put a payload on them. Video coming soon!

faq.question: What do you mean by a stack in this series?
faq.answer: The combination of resources that host your application — compute, database, queue, storage, DNS, and maybe a load balancer later. Not every SaaS bolt-on like Stripe. More the place your internal or office apps actually run.

faq.question: Why build your own stack instead of using Railway or Supabase?
faq.answer: Those services are amazing. They also add up once you have a lot of ideas, multiple environments, or you are building something like an internet of apps. Building your own stack with tools like Terraform gives you predictable pricing and a place you control when you start wiring other systems in.

faq.question: Why does this matter for integrating other systems and AI agents?
faq.answer: When cloud-managed agents or third-party services need to talk into your AWS or other cloud setup, you need secure networking and a clear target. Containers help you keep things updated and scale. That pays off when you understand the stack underneath instead of only clicking through managed dashboards.

faq.question: What is the classic stack in this first lesson?
faq.answer: A Linux box with Docker: Laravel for the app, Redis and Horizon for queues, Postgres with migrations, and storage on volumes so uploads survive deploys. Terraform stands it up. GitHub runs tests and deploys with zero downtime and no clickOps.

faq.question: Are you using RDS, SQS, and S3 in this first lesson?
faq.answer: No. This first lesson is just a Linux box — which is what a lot of managed services are underneath anyway. Dedicated cloud databases, queues, and object storage are options later. The next article covers hosting multiple apps on one box.

faq.question: Do I need to be a Linux expert to follow along?
faq.answer: You need some basic Linux, including things like SSH. Do not panic about it. AI can help, even when it is wrong, and you can ask questions on the post. The goal is to grow through this together, not to assume you already know every command.

data.title: Why I No Longer Build With n8n
data.excerpt: I used to build my back ends in n8n - APIs, background jobs, queue work, AI integration, all of it. Something happened in January 2026 and now I don't reach for it, or for no-code platforms, at all. Here's the walls I hit and what I build with instead.

children.text: TLDR

This is about why I think products like n8n and no-code platforms are going to struggle - and it’s coming from someone who had a podcast on them, numerous videos, blogposts and even introduced n8n to Pfizer and other companies. Something happened in January 2026 that pretty much changed the game, and I don’t know if there’s any going back.
Why I chose these tools in the first place
🤯 2024 I was trying to figure this out
https://laravel-news.com/php-and-llms-with-alfred-nutile
So let’s talk about why I chose these tools a year or more ago, when AI was first coming around. About three years ago, say, I wrote a book
LLMs and PHP
, and n8n snuck into that book because I went from building with code to building with n8n. And you’ll see that it was that moment where I could say, listen: code is debt.

If I write a project and it has code, there’s going to be a certain overhead of writing that code. No matter how many libraries I use. Shipping that code, deploying it, maintaining it and whatnot. And to a degree that stayed quite true for the work I was doing.

And when I hit the moments that I’m going to explain here - I don’t want to call them edge cases, because I forget the term, but once everything’s an edge case, then what is it, right? It still was worth it, because it was better than code, in my opinion, when it came to those factors.

Now, you can still write beautiful UIs and user integrations or applications. But when writing the back end, I was starting to just write it in n8n, or build it in n8n. Back ends, APIs, background processes, queue work - all of it was there. And most importantly at the time, was AI integration.

Integrating to AI was a big deal back then for me. And being a PHP person, it was even scarier, because there wasn’t a community around that at the time. And it was just that moment: where do I stick to PHP and code? Where am I gonna go? Is it Python? Is it something else? n8n was pretty awesome at the LangChain and other stuff.
Then you start hitting walls

So after a year of using it or more, and implementing it in places, I’m like, yeah, it’s great. But then you start hitting walls, whether it’s n8n or Activepieces or whatever your platform is. These backend systems have their limitations.

Processing large files was a big one. Processing large amounts of data, and rows of data, was a big one. Scaling to numerous traffic, incoming data, can be tedious. Long-running processes, processes that you break down in half and loop through - but you cannot easily have more than one loop in a workflow, because you just run into issues (memory and count).

So I had to work around a lot of these. Anyone who’s working in it long enough knows those limitations. And even things in the free version with n8n - sure, you can connect to your Gmail. But when you’re writing a workflow that needs to connect to the Gmail of the person using the workflow from a remote system, then yeah, it gets hard. It gets tricky. And I’m sure, again, their paid version offers things, and I’m sure, again, you can do some magic with it.

But these things became a reality. Testing. How do we deploy this without testing? AI’s getting amazing at n8n it, too - then I can give AI existing n8n systems and say, go fix what’s going on. So there are a lot of moments where it’s still working okay. But to be honest, it’s because of these reasons I’m removing it as much as possible too.
What I reach for now
So now let’s talk about that. When building a new application, no matter what, do I reach for n8n? Do I reach for no-code platforms like Softr? And the answer is never, no.
I made a starter template for my projects so getting started is that easy
https://github.com/alnutile/supabse-vibecoding-starter

Those platforms always had limitations. No-code systems do not have a database that can scale. Airtable just couldn’t scale - millions of records, processing JSON and complex data queries, indexing, vectorizing, hybrid search. None of that stuff worked. And so the moment your product would scale is the moment you were stretching the limits of what you could do, and compromising. It just never worked to that point.
I think these companies are realizing that as well, as they deal with introducing vibe coding and other things to their framework to compensate for the fact that this is a reality.

So when I have a new application, I have templates I can use to build them out. With authentication. Event systems. Storage. Database. I lean on Supabase, but there’s so many others out there, Neon and others. The foundation of authentication and permissions is too easy out of the box.

Deploying these things is just too easy out of the box as well. Railway, or Vercel. So many options. Lovable, Replit. I mean, the list goes on. Replit’s a great example, too. Why would you choose these no-code tools over a Replit, when you can just have it do these things for you out of the box? Authentication. Build out UIs that are nice and consistent. They don’t break, because it can build this stuff. It can test this stuff. And there is not I can not do that here moments.

As far as integrations go and connections, those are great, and many of them are already ready to go. But to be fair, this stuff’s getting so easy that you can prompt that in a moment. It’s really not that hard so they can’t be as much of a selling point anymore to the systems.

So when I have a project that needs a UI or needs to process large files, I would never reach for any of that ever again. I’d rather just have Claude, Open Router, Cursor, OpenAI and some harness and build a Python script that can process the file the moment it hits a Lambda S3 bucket - but it doesn’t have to be a Lambda function, because those have their own limitations. So I could just put that in Railway or some other service like Railway that can just run that Python script on an event.
The translation factor

I think in the end these products just can’t last, because - if anything - the translation factor between the business requirements and the outcome gets too compromised. When the business requirements are X and clearly defined, and I can give that to Claude and it can build it, then why would you put it through a filter that compromises or alters what’s possible?
And that, to me, comes back to the point:
code is no longer debt

. If I can have automations maintaining it. Doing security audits on it. Building it in the background. Showing me - you know, I can do QA still, but doing the QA for me at a level I used to write by hand, because I’ve always been TDD or close enough.

Now I can have proper CI/CD deploying to production with confidence. Now I know I can roll forward into proper DORA.dev project statistics on my projects. Now I can get back to that kind of pattern. You’ll even see a video
here
where I’m coding inside of the application, or building features, by just making a card and putting it onto a lane so it builds it.
n8n is easier to use for the non builder

This is not even a question any more nor has it ever been. The best builders today know the business domain and enough about getting from build to deploy that the transition from business goal to deployed product has zero loss. N8N was never easy to use and bad builders built bad complex too big workflows eg the same spaghetti code I use to build years ago. So this just never was true nor even close any more since we are not longer thinking at the code level but more “what is the business goal”.
Who should still reach for what

So, if you’re a company or a person struggling with building things, then heck no, never choose these other products. You would choose a Replit, because then you can do the vibe coding and get the CI/CD pipeline out of it, with the databases and authentication already done and clear and working.

Never settle for anything else, like no-code platforms because you’re just not going to get that flexibility. You’re going to get limitations. Postgres doesn’t have limitations other than your budget. I mean, that’s the bottom line. You’re gonna choose a database like Postgres and never look back, or you’re going to add to that database DuckDB etc. You know, you’re going to extend it with other databases. You’re not going to look back and be like, darn, I can’t do this because it’s a million rows or 10 million rows. It just doesn’t matter. You’re not gonna say, I can’t do this, because you chose JavaScript.

I mean, that’s the thing. So with Replit you can scale, of course, if you have budget. But then, if you’re more confident in your company, that knows how to do the infrastructure stuff, the CI/CD, the Azure, the AWS, whatever it takes to bring all these pieces together securely in your own private cloud, or connecting securely from service to service to your cloud - then again, you wouldn’t choose Replit necessarily. You would choose just a normal, vanilla type solution that is optimized for your company.

So that every time something’s built, Claude or OpenAI or your harness of choice, Cursor, starts off with that particular templated platform that you have to just get going. Not your own Lovable as much as your own established patterns, skills, and methodologies to just build out a good solid system quickly and easily with confidence. And that again, it takes that extra level of expertise. But if Replit’s holding you back, then you do that.
Where I’ve landed

But yeah, I mean, this is it. This is it moving forward. It means saying, hey, time to move on. And I think, you know, I’m glad I used those things back then. I’m glad I gave up on coding back then. Because now I see I don’t need to code to benefit from code. And code is no longer debt, so I get the best of both worlds, to be honest with you.
All right, I just wanted to share that. And hopefully it helps people kind of think this through. If you have any questions, ask below. Any topics you want to cover, ask below. Thank you.

faq.question: Why stop building back ends in n8n?
faq.answer: The walls show up once the work gets real: processing large files, processing large amounts of rows, scaling to heavy incoming traffic, long-running processes, and the fact that you cannot easily run more than one loop in a workflow without hitting memory and count issues. Add testing and deployment on top of that, and the workarounds start to outweigh what the platform saves you.

faq.question: Is code still technical debt?
faq.answer: No, and that is the shift. Automations can maintain it, run security audits on it, build features in the background, and do a level of QA that used to be hand-written. With proper CI/CD deploying to production, code stops being the liability it was and becomes the flexible option again.

faq.question: What do you build with instead of n8n or no-code platforms?
faq.answer: A template project on Supabase or something like Neon, with authentication, permissions, an event system, storage, and a database out of the box, deployed to Railway or Vercel. For file processing, a Python script triggered on an event rather than a workflow node. Claude, OpenRouter, Cursor, OpenAI and a harness do the building.

faq.question: Can no-code databases like Airtable scale?
faq.answer: Not to the point most real products need. Millions of records, complex JSON and data queries, indexing, vectorizing, hybrid search — those were the limits hit in practice. Postgres has no limitation other than budget, and it can be extended with something like DuckDB when needed.

faq.question: Isn't n8n easier for people who don't build?
faq.answer: It was never actually easy. Bad builders built big, complex, spaghetti workflows the same way bad code got written years ago. The best builders today know the business domain and enough about going from build to deploy that there is no loss in translation, and the thinking happens at the business-goal level rather than the code level.

faq.question: Who should use Replit versus their own cloud setup?
faq.answer: If you or your company struggle with building and infrastructure, Replit gives you vibe coding plus a CI/CD pipeline, database, and authentication already working. If your company already knows the infrastructure, CI/CD, and cloud security side, you would skip Replit and use your own established patterns, skills, and templates optimized for how you build.

data.title: An Ambient Slack Agent You Actually Build Yourself
data.excerpt: Taking the agent from the last video and plugging it into a Slack room so it listens to everything, remembers it, and wakes up a real Linux box when it needs to. Supabase for the route and the memory, Railway for the box, Zapier's SDK for the CRM.
